identification.summary: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM) is a China-linked cyberespionage actor. It first became known for compromising telecommunications providers by exploiting unpatched internet-facing services such as WildFly/JBoss, then deploying web shells and off-the-shelf credential and lateral-movement tools [S1]. In June 2022 Unit 42 reported that the group had expanded beyond telecommunications to financial institutions and government entities and was using a new RAT, PingPull [S2]. In 2023 Unit 42 tied the same cluster (Alloy Taurus) to a Linux PingPull variant and a new backdoor, Sword2033 [S3]. It also attributed, with moderate confidence, one of three China-nexus clusters active against a Southeast Asian government to Alloy Taurus [S4].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE and Unit 42 describe the group as active since at least 2012 [S5]. Microsoft's 2019 report covered activity observed mainly from 2018 to mid-2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM). The Hacker News coverage of Unit 42's September 2023 report gives Granite Typhoon as an alias for Alloy Taurus, while Unit 42's own report lists GALLIUM [S4]. In Microsoft's taxonomy, 'Typhoon' indicates origin or attribution to China [S9]. Unit 42 tracks the group as Alloy Taurus and describes Alloy Taurus as also known as GALLIUM and Softcell [S2]. MITRE tracks it as GALLIUM (G0093) [S5]. Cluster boundary caution: SentinelLabs assessed the 2023 Middle East telecom intrusions as highly likely the work of a Chinese cyberespionage group in the nexus of Gallium and APT41, with the exact grouping unclear [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (vendor assessments only; no government attribution found in the sources gathered). MITRE describes GALLIUM as likely Chinese state-sponsored [S5]. Unit 42 calls the group a likely Chinese state-sponsored group, citing its geographic and sector focus, technical skill and use of known Chinese threat-actor malware and TTPs [S2].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only, at the 'likely' level [S2][S5]. Microsoft's 2019 GALLIUM report does not attribute the group to a specific state [S1]; Microsoft's later 'Typhoon' name signals China origin or attribution under its taxonomy [S9]. Unit 42 attributed its 2023 Southeast Asian government cluster (CL-STA-0045) to Alloy Taurus with moderate confidence [S4].
attribution.basis: Tooling overlap with known Chinese actors, including China Chopper, Poison Ivy and Gh0st-derived malware [S1][S2]; consistent targeting of telecommunications and government entities [S2]; infrastructure hosted in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan [S1].

objectives: Intelligence collection from telecommunications providers [S1][S2]. Targeting later widened to government and financial entities, consistent with broader espionage [S2][S4].

sectors: Financial institutions and public financial administrators [S2][S4]
Critical infrastructure and public healthcare (Southeast Asian government cluster, shared across three actors) [S4]
regions: Southeast Asia, Europe and Africa (historic telecom targeting) [S2]
Afghanistan, Australia, Belgium, Cambodia, Malaysia, Mozambique, the Philippines, Russia and Vietnam (entities linked to 2022 infrastructure) [S2]
An unnamed Southeast Asian government (Alloy Taurus cluster activity from early 2022 into 2023) [S4]
South Africa and Nepal (2023 Linux PingPull/Sword2033 activity) [S3]
Middle East telecommunications providers (Q1 2023; SentinelLabs places the actor in the Gallium/APT41 nexus) [S8]
targeting.notes: Telecommunications has been the most consistent focus [S1][S2]. Unit 42's 2022 country list comes from targeted entities tied to GALLIUM infrastructure, not confirmed compromises [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is mainly through exploiting unpatched internet-facing services, notably WildFly/JBoss, with public exploits; this needs no phishing or user interaction [S1]. In later activity Unit 42 and SentinelLabs reported exploitation of Exchange servers [S4][S8]. After access, the group installs web shells (China Chopper and BlackMould, a native IIS web shell based on China Chopper) and moves laterally mainly with compromised domain credentials and PsExec [S1]. Common tools are HTRAN, Mimikatz, NBTScan, Netcat, PsExec, Windows Credential Editor and WinRAR [S1]. Malware includes a modified Poison Ivy that Microsoft said appeared unique to GALLIUM and QuarkBandit, a modified Gh0st RAT. The group changed their communications to evade existing signatures, installed SoftEther VPN on internal systems for persistence, and signed at least one credential dumper with a stolen certificate [S1]. PingPull (2022) is a RAT with variants using ICMP, HTTP(S) or raw TCP for C2; its ICMP use exploits the fact that few organizations inspect ICMP [S2]. In 2023 the group added a Linux PingPull variant, which only 3 of 62 vendors flagged when it was reported, and the Sword2033 backdoor for file upload, download and command execution [S3].

campaigns.name: GALLIUM telecom intrusions (Microsoft)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported GALLIUM exploiting WildFly/JBoss and using web shells, Mimikatz, PsExec, SoftEther VPN and modified Poison Ivy and Gh0st-variant malware against telecommunications providers, mainly from 2018 to mid-2019.

campaigns.name: PingPull expansion
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported the new PingPull RAT and expansion to government and finance targets, with infrastructure linked to entities in nine countries.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government intrusions (CL-STA-0045)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 attributed CL-STA-0045, one of three China-nexus clusters active against the same Southeast Asian government, to Alloy Taurus with moderate confidence; the activity began in early 2022, continued through 2023, and exploited Exchange servers to deploy web shells for long-term espionage.

campaigns.name: Operation Tainted Love (Middle East telecoms)
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs reported Q1 2023 intrusions against Middle East telecom providers through internet-facing Exchange servers, with custom Mimikatz-based credential theft (mim221). It assessed the activity as an evolution of Operation Soft Cell tooling and judged it highly likely to be a Chinese cyberespionage group in the nexus of Gallium and APT41, with the exact grouping unclear.

campaigns.name: Linux PingPull and Sword2033
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported a Linux PingPull variant and the new Sword2033 backdoor used against targets in South Africa and Nepal.

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage operators that vendors assess as likely state-sponsored [S2][S5]. No named individuals or units appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Public exploits for internet-facing servers; China Chopper and BlackMould web shells; Mimikatz, WCE, PsExec and HTRAN; modified Poison Ivy and QuarkBandit; PingPull for Windows and Linux; Sword2033 [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 mainly on dynamic DNS subdomains (ddns.net, myftp.biz); domains hosted in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan; Taiwan-based servers, apparently exclusive to GALLIUM, used for web shell connections [S1]; SoftEther VPN inside victim networks [S1].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications providers, government entities and financial institutions in Southeast Asia, Europe, Africa and elsewhere [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Government targeting supports broader intelligence requirements [S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing application and mail servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) and networks that do not inspect ICMP [S1][S2][S8].

gaps: No Unit 42 primary reports could be fetched (2022 PingPull, 2023 Linux PingPull, 2023 SE Asia clusters); facts come from search-result summaries and press coverage [S2][S3][S4].

Microsoft's threat-actor naming table could not be opened, and Microsoft's 2023 taxonomy post does not list Granite Typhoon. The Granite Typhoon = Alloy Taurus mapping relies on press coverage of Unit 42 reporting [S4][S9].

Neither the MITRE ATT&CK page nor the SentinelLabs page could be fetched; content relies on search-result coverage [S5][S8]. Cybereason's Operation Soft Cell reporting (2019) was not included because no verified source URL was retained.

Cluster boundary: Unit 42 treats Softcell as a GALLIUM alias, while SentinelLabs placed 2023 Middle East activity in the Gallium/APT41 nexus. Shared or leaked tooling (Poison Ivy, China Chopper, Mimikatz) limits confidence in these links [S2][S8].
The CrowdStrike alias PHANTOM PANDA and the imported 'Red Dev 4' alias were not confirmed in any source opened.
No government attribution, indictment, sanctions or joint advisory naming this group was found. The sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is unknown.
No well-sourced activity after 2023 was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (define the OE): Key terrain is telecom provider networks that hold call detail records, plus internet-facing application and mail servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) at telecom, government and finance entities [S1][S2][S8]. STEP 2 (describe effects): Unpatched public-facing services give a foothold with no user interaction, and ICMP-based C2 can evade networks that do not inspect ICMP [S1][S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): the actor exploits a public-facing server, installs a China Chopper or BlackMould web shell, harvests credentials with Mimikatz or WCE, moves laterally with PsExec, persists with RATs (PingPull, Poison Ivy, QuarkBandit) or SoftEther VPN, and stages data with WinRAR [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained, low-cost collection of subscriber metadata and government data from partner-nation telecom and government networks [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: new web shells on IIS or JBoss servers; anomalous ICMP payloads; SoftEther VPN on servers; C2 on dynamic DNS (ddns.net, myftp.biz); tools signed with stolen certificates; Linux hosts beaconing over HTTPS to unfamiliar domains [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track exploitation of internet-facing servers and ICMP C2 patterns across DoD-adjacent and partner telecom networks in regions the group has targeted (Southeast Asia, Africa, Europe, Middle East) [S1][S2][S8]. Authorities: most of the targeted terrain is commercial or partner-nation telecom outside the DODIN, so response depends on partner nations and private providers rather than direct DoD action [S2]. Coordination: share indicators (web shells, PingPull, Sword2033, dynamic DNS C2) with partner CERTs and providers, and reconcile vendor names (Granite Typhoon, GALLIUM, Alloy Taurus, Softcell) in shared reporting without merging the APT41 cluster [S1][S2][S3][S8].
